content:
Short answer

The honest answer is uncomfortable: a true superintelligence could, in principle, do almost any job better and cheaper than a human, so no occupation is permanently "safe". But jobs will not all disappear at once. Work done entirely on a computer (data entry, coding, writing, analysis, customer service) is exposed first; jobs needing robots in messy physical environments (plumbing, nursing care, construction) come later because robotics lags behind software; and jobs where people want a human for trust, accountability or connection last longest. What you do matters: people who learn to direct AI, own assets, build trusted relationships and work in physical or human-centred roles will be far better placed. This guide ranks more than 150 jobs by risk, explains why, and gives a concrete action plan.

Read this first: what this article can and cannot tell you

  • Nobody knows exact timelines. Superintelligence (SI) might arrive within years, decades or not on current paths. See how we could achieve superintelligence.
  • "Can be automated" is not "will be replaced". Cost, regulation, liability, customer preference, unions and physical bottlenecks all slow replacement.
  • Jobs are bundles of tasks. AI usually automates tasks first, changing jobs before eliminating them. A job with 70% automatable tasks might shrink headcount rather than vanish.
  • Risk ratings below assume capable AI agents and, later, SI-level systems with advancing robotics. They describe direction and order, not certainties.

What the evidence already shows

Even before superintelligence, today's AI is changing work:

  • OpenAI and University of Pennsylvania researchers estimated in 2023 that about 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected by large language models, and about 19% could see at least half of their tasks affected.
  • The IMF estimated in 2024 that almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, rising to about 60% in advanced economies.
  • The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 projected 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced worldwide by 2030, a net gain of 78 million, with clerical roles among the fastest declining.
  • Stanford Digital Economy Lab researchers found that early-career workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations were employed roughly 19% below where they would have been had they kept pace with less-exposed peers, while experienced workers showed no comparable gap.

The pattern so far: entry-level, routine cognitive work is hit first. Superintelligence would extend this to expert work.

Why superintelligence is different from past automation

Past technologies automated specific tasks (spinning thread, calculating, assembling cars), and workers moved to tasks machines could not do. Superintelligence threatens to automate the ability to learn new tasks itself. That is why it is different:

The main brake is the physical world: robots, factories, energy and regulation move slower than software. See what superintelligence could do, and its limits.

The five factors that decide a job's risk

1. Digital vs physical: is the work done on a screen, or with hands in unpredictable places? 2. Routine vs novel: does it follow patterns, or require handling truly new situations? 3. Verifiable output: can the result be checked easily (code passes tests, numbers reconcile)? Easily checked work is automated faster. 4. Human preference and trust: do customers want a human, for empathy, accountability or status? 5. Regulation and liability: must a licensed human sign off (doctors, lawyers, pilots, judges)?

The risk scale used below

Waves: Wave 1 = advanced AI agents and early SI (digital work). Wave 2 = SI plus capable robotics (physical work). Wave 3 = roles protected mainly by human preference and law.

1. Office, administrative and support jobs

2. Technology and software jobs

3. Finance, accounting and insurance

4. Legal jobs

5. Creative, media and marketing jobs

6. Education jobs

7. Healthcare jobs

8. Science, engineering and research

9. Sales and retail

10. Transport and logistics

11. Manufacturing and skilled trades

12. Hospitality and food

13. Agriculture and environment

14. Public sector, safety and security

15. Management and business

16. Personal care, community and meaning

The pattern across all 150+ jobs

The uncomfortable twist: many well-paid, highly educated jobs are more exposed than many lower-paid manual jobs. That reverses the pattern of earlier automation waves. This is sometimes called Moravec's paradox: tasks that are hard for humans, like advanced maths, can be easier for machines than tasks that are easy for humans, like folding laundry.

What to do: an honest action plan

For everyone

1. Become fluent with AI tools now. People who use AI well will replace people who do not, long before AI replaces everyone. Learn prompting, AI agents and the tools in your field. 2. Move from doing to deciding. Aim for roles where you are accountable for outcomes, not just producing outputs. 3. Build trust capital. A reputation, network and relationships are hard to automate. Clients hire people they know. 4. Develop physical or human-presence skills as a hedge: a trade, care skills, teaching, coaching or hospitality. 5. Build financial resilience. Keep an emergency fund, reduce high-interest debt, and diversify income sources. 6. Own assets, not just labour. If AI makes labour cheaper, returns may flow to owners of businesses, property, intellectual property and productive capital. This is general information, not financial advice; speak to a qualified adviser about your own situation. 7. Stay adaptable. Expect to change roles more than once. Learning how to learn is the core skill. 8. Protect your wellbeing. Rapid change is stressful. Community, health and purpose outside work matter more than ever.

For students

  • Choose fields that combine technical understanding with human-facing or physical work: healthcare, skilled trades, engineering with field work, teaching, or AI safety and governance.
  • Learn to work alongside AI in whatever you study.
  • Gain real-world experience early, because entry-level roles are being squeezed first.
  • Avoid paying heavily for degrees that train only for highly automatable tasks.

For mid-career workers

  • Map your job's tasks: which could AI do now, which in five years, which need you?
  • Become the person in your organisation who knows how to apply AI to your team's work.
  • Move towards client-facing, supervisory or accountable parts of your role.
  • Consider adjacent moves into roles with lower risk ratings in the tables above.

For business owners and freelancers

  • Use AI to cut costs before competitors do, but invest the savings in what AI cannot easily copy: brand, customer relationships, proprietary data and quality.
  • Shift from selling hours to selling outcomes.
  • If your service is mostly digital production (writing, design, data processing, billing, coding), assume prices will fall and differentiate through expertise, accountability and trust.

For governments and employers

  • Fund retraining at scale, especially for entry-level and mid-career workers.
  • Explore income support options, from wage insurance to universal basic income pilots.
  • Consider broader ownership of AI gains through public investment funds, profit-sharing or taxation of AI rents.
  • Protect workers' rights around AI monitoring and decision-making.
  • Plan transitions with unions and communities rather than imposing them suddenly.

Honest scenarios for the future of work

See positive and negative impacts of superintelligence and what happens after superintelligence for the wider picture.

Frequently asked questions

Which jobs are completely safe from superintelligence?

Honestly, none are guaranteed safe forever. Jobs combining physical dexterity in unpredictable environments, deep human trust and legal accountability, such as nurses, electricians, plumbers, social workers, care workers, paramedics and clergy, are likely to last longest.

Will superintelligence cause mass unemployment?

It could, if capabilities arrive quickly and gains are not shared. History shows technology usually creates new jobs, but superintelligence may also do the new jobs. Policy choices will decide whether displacement means hardship or freedom.

How soon will my job be affected?

Digital, routine jobs are already changing. Wider effects depend on how fast AI agents and robotics improve. Watch for signals such as AI completing multi-day tasks reliably and robots working in unstructured environments. See how we could achieve superintelligence for the signs to monitor.

Should I still learn to code?

Yes, but as a way to understand and direct technology, not as a guaranteed career on its own. Combining coding with domain expertise, product thinking or AI oversight is far more durable.

What new jobs will superintelligence create?

Likely growth areas include AI oversight and safety, robot maintenance, energy and data center construction, human-centred care, experience design, and roles we cannot yet name. Whether these absorb displaced workers at scale is uncertain.
